feed.title: NPR Topics: Science
feed.subtitle: Explore scientific breakthroughs, space discoveries, research trends and everyday mysteries with NPR’s science team. Plus episodes from the Short Wave podcast.

entry.title: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust
entry.summary: As it races to develop its new massive rocket, the space launch company is preparing to retire NASA's main ride to the International Space Station.

entry.title: This week in science: PTSD prediction, phishing while tired, an exoplanet
entry.summary: The regular news roundup with NPR's science podcast Short Wave covers a possible use for AI in emergency rooms, a distant planet and the link between cybersecurity and Daylight Saving Time.

entry.title: Scientists think they've found ancient remnants of dinosaur blood
entry.summary: Scientists have studied plenty of dinosaur bones, eggs and footprints. Now, some think they've found their strongest evidence yet of dinosaur blood.

entry.title: Mice can learn to fight by watching tiny rodent cage matches, study finds
entry.summary: Brain scientists set up "gladiator style" cage matches for mice — and found that simply observing fighting matches can rewire a mouse's brain to resemble those who actually fought.

entry.title: He was diagnosed with cancer. Then he was told he lost his Medicaid
entry.summary: Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout of Medicaid work requirements has been rife with problems.

entry.title: NASA is looking for astronauts to live and work on the Moon
entry.summary: NASA needs more recruits in order to return to the moon after being gone more than half a century.

entry.title: Climate change is altering the colors we see in the world: an illustrated journey
entry.summary: From Arctic landscapes to insect bodies, climate change is shifting the familiar colors of nature.

entry.title: How octopuses squeeze through teeny tiny holes
entry.summary: Robots used during search and rescue operations need to be able to wriggle through narrow cracks and crevices. Researchers have turned to a natural contortionist for inspiration — the octopus.

entry.title: Oyster stocks have plunged in the Chesapeake. This resident wants to bring them back
entry.summary: Oyster reefs once abounded in the Chesapeake, but overharvesting slashed their populations, leading to poorer water quality and less habitat for other species. Now, researchers and local residents are finding creative ways to bring their numbers back up.

entry.title: This week in science: mysterious X-rays, movement and learning, and memory formation
entry.summary: Emily Kwong and Ari Daniel of NPR's Short Wave talk about mysterious X-ray objects, the link between movement and learning and how a small part of the brain triggers memory formation.
